WalkthroughText: When you call a non-void method, Java pushes a brand-new stack frame for that method, runs its code, and computes a value at the return statement. That returned value flies back to the exact spot where the method was called, and then the frame is popped (destroyed). If you want to keep that value, you must assign the call expression to a variable in the caller's own frame — otherwise the value is discarded forever. This walkthrough traces a call to a method that doubles a number, showing the caller's frame, the callee's frame, and exactly how the return value travels back.

PracticeItems.Explanation: Since square returns an int, you must capture that value by assigning the call to a variable of matching type, as in int ans = square(5);. Option B reverses the assignment illegally, option C never stores the returned value (it's discarded), and option D uses 'void' which cannot hold a returned int value.
triple(4) returns 12, so a = 12. triple(2) returns 6. b = a + 6 = 12 + 6 = 18. A common mistake (12) forgets to add the second call's return value, and 6 only reflects the second call alone.

Choices: Because x is a local variable inside getValue's stack frame and no longer exists once getValue returns, so main cannot access it
Because getValue() must be assigned to a variable before it can run
Because return statements are not allowed inside non-void methods
PracticeItems.Explanation: When getValue() finishes executing, its stack frame (including the local variable x) is popped off the call stack and destroyed. The variable x in main's println refers to a completely different scope, so it doesn't exist there — this is a scope/compile error. It is perfectly legal to call getValue() without using its return value; the error is about accessing x outside its frame.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: We start in main's stack frame, about to call doubleIt(5) and store the result in a variable named ans.
main declares ans, but it has no value yet — the call to doubleIt(5) hasn't finished.
Java pauses main and pushes a brand-new stack frame for doubleIt, passing in 5 as the parameter n.
Inside doubleIt's own frame, a local variable result is computed as n times 2, which is 10.
The return statement sends the value of result — 10 — back to wherever doubleIt was called from.
Now that doubleIt has finished and returned its value, its entire stack frame — including n and result — is popped and destroyed.
Back in main's frame, the returned value 10 is assigned into ans, completing the statement.
main's frame now holds ans = 10 permanently, while doubleIt's local variables no longer exist anywhere — the return value was the only thing that survived the call.
